pharm: Pegylated RNA aptamer that selectively binds extracellular VEGF-165, blocking its interaction with VEGF receptors and inhibiting pathologic ocular neovascularization and vascular permeability.
quick: 0.3 mg by intravitreal injection into the affected eye once every 6 weeks
Limited data; use only if clearly needed (minimal systemic exposure)
Unknown if excreted in milk; use caution
Intraocular pressure, perfusion of optic nerve, signs of endophthalmitis/infection after injection
summary: Pegaptanib sodium is a pegylated anti-VEGF RNA aptamer administered by intravitreal injection for the treatment of neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration. It selectively binds the VEGF-165 isoform, inhibiting abnormal blood vessel growth and vascular leakage in the retina. The main risks are procedure-related ocular complications, most importantly endophthalmitis, as well as retinal detachment, traumatic cataract, and increased intraocular pressure. Strict aseptic injection technique and post-injection monitoring for endophthalmitis are essential.
indications: Treatment of neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration

dosage.d: 0.3 mg (in 90 microliters) injected into the vitreous of the affected eye once every 6 weeks (9 times per year)
dosage.n: Single-use prefilled syringe; one eye per session

dosage.d: Resume the every-6-week schedule as soon as feasible
dosage.n: Do not give two injections to catch up

admin: Administer only by a qualified ophthalmologist using strict aseptic technique
Use adequate anesthesia and a broad-spectrum microbicide before injection
Inject into the vitreous cavity 3.5-4.0 mm posterior to the limbus, avoiding the horizontal meridian and aiming toward the center of the globe
Monitor intraocular pressure and optic nerve head perfusion immediately after injection
Instruct patients to report symptoms of endophthalmitis (eye pain, redness, photophobia, blurred vision) without delay
moa: Pegaptanib is a covalently pegylated oligonucleotide aptamer that adopts a three-dimensional conformation enabling it to bind with high specificity and affinity to the heparin-binding domain of the VEGF-165 isoform of vascular endothelial growth factor. By sequestering extracellular VEGF-165, it prevents VEGF from binding to its receptors (VEGFR-1 and VEGFR-2) on vascular endothelial cells. This suppresses the pathologic angiogenesis and increased vascular permeability that characterize neovascular AMD, while having less effect on physiologic VEGF isoforms (e.g., VEGF-121).

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to pegaptanib or any excipient
monitor: Signs of endophthalmitis and retinal detachment in the week following injection

preg: Systemic exposure after intravitreal injection is very low. There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women; animal data showed effects only at high systemic doses. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
lact: It is not known whether pegaptanib is excreted in human milk. Because systemic exposure is minimal, risk to a nursing infant is expected to be low, but caution is advised when administering to a breastfeeding woman.
renal: Mild to moderate renal impairment does not require dose adjustment; systemic exposure is negligible after intravitreal administration. No data in severe renal impairment, but a clinically significant effect is not anticipated.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required. Negligible systemic exposure makes a clinically significant effect of hepatic impairment unlikely.

minor: No systemic drug-drug interaction studies have been performed; clinically significant systemic interactions are not expected given minimal systemic absorption
interactions.food: Not applicable; administered by intravitreal injection.
interactions.diagnostics: No significant laboratory test interference; ocular imaging used to assess response.

emergency: Acute severe intraocular pressure elevation with optic nerve compromise

monitoring: Intraocular pressure immediately and shortly after each injection
Optic nerve head perfusion after injection
Signs and symptoms of endophthalmitis during the week after injection
Visual acuity and retinal status at follow-up visits
counsel: This medicine is injected into the eye by your ophthalmologist about every 6 weeks
Seek care immediately if your eye becomes painful or red, more sensitive to light, or your vision worsens after injection - these may signal a serious infection
Some floaters, mild eye discomfort, or a red spot on the white of the eye are common and usually settle
Do not rub the eye and follow any antibiotic drop instructions after the injection
Keep all scheduled injection and follow-up appointments to protect your vision
pk: Begins binding ocular VEGF after injection; clinical benefit over weeks
Slow absorption from vitreous into systemic circulation; very low plasma levels
Approximately 10 days in plasma after intravitreal dosing
Therapeutic vitreous levels support dosing every 6 weeks
Refrigerate at 2-8 C; do not freeze; protect prefilled syringe from light
pearls: Selective for the VEGF-165 isoform, unlike pan-VEGF agents (ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept)
Key procedural risk is endophthalmitis - emphasize aseptic technique and prompt reporting of eye pain/redness/vision loss
Largely superseded by more effective pan-VEGF agents but still labeled for wet AMD
Monitor intraocular pressure and optic nerve perfusion immediately after each injection
Minimal systemic exposure means no renal or hepatic dose adjustment
missed: Pegaptanib is given by an ophthalmologist on a fixed schedule (every 6 weeks). If you miss an appointment, contact your eye doctor to reschedule as soon as possible; the injection is not self-administered.
overdose: Intravitreal doses higher than recommended have been administered without unexpected adverse effects. Overdose primarily raises local ocular risk; manage by monitoring intraocular pressure and optic nerve perfusion and providing supportive ophthalmic care.
